docs.text: Operation Complexity Access \(O(1)\) Update \(O(1)\) Traverse \(O(n)\) Linear search \(O(n)\) Binary search \(O(\log n)\) Append \(O(1)\) amortized Insert at beginning \(O(n)\) Insert at middle \(O(n)\) Delete at beginning \(O(n)\) Delete at middle \(O(n)\) Delete at end \(O(1)\) Reverse \(O(n)\) Sort \(O(n\log n)\) typical comparison sort

docs.title: 9. Important Array Patterns
docs.text:
Most LeetCode and competitive-programming array problems are not solved by knowing more syntax.

They are solved by recognizing structure.

The major patterns are:

Arrays
├── Basic traversal
├── Frequency counting
├── Prefix/Suffix
├── Two pointers
├── Sliding window
├── Binary search
├── Sorting + scanning
├── Hashing
├── Kadane's algorithm
├── Difference arrays
├── Intervals
├── Monotonic stack
├── Monotonic deque
├── Greedy
├── Dynamic programming
├── Divide and conquer
├── Bit manipulation
├── Cyclic placement
├── Coordinate compression
├── Sweep line
└── Matrix techniques

docs.title: 10. Pattern: Basic Traversal
docs.text:
The simplest array pattern.

for x in nums:
    ...

Use when:

  • every element must be inspected,
  • the answer can be maintained incrementally,
  • no special ordering is required.

Typical examples:

  • maximum element,
  • minimum element,
  • sum,
  • count,
  • frequency,
  • validation.

docs.title: Running State
docs.text:
Instead of storing everything, maintain only what is necessary.

maximum = float("-inf")

for x in nums:
    maximum = max(maximum, x)

Complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

Time:

\[ O(n) \]

Space:

\[ O(1) \]

docs.title: 11. Pattern: Frequency Counting
docs.text:
When values belong to a manageable domain, count occurrences.

freq = {}

for x in nums:
    freq[x] = freq.get(x, 0) + 1

Useful for:

  • duplicates,
  • anagrams,
  • frequency comparisons,
  • majority elements,
  • counting pairs.

Complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

average time with hashing.

docs.title: Frequency Array
docs.text:
If:

\[ 0\le x < k \]

and \(k\) is reasonably small:

freq = [0] * k

for x in nums:
    freq[x] += 1

This can be preferable to hashing.

Complexity:

\[ O(n+k) \]

docs.title: 12. Pattern: Prefix Sum
docs.text:
Define:

\[ P[i]=\sum_{j=0}^{i}A[j] \]

Example:

A = [3, 1, 4, 2]

P = [3, 4, 8, 10]

Range sum:

\[ \sum_{i=l}^{r}A[i] = P[r]-P[l-1] \]

for \(l>0\).

With a leading zero:

prefix = [0]

for x in nums:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)

Then:

\[ \boxed{ \operatorname{sum}(l,r) = P[r+1]-P[l] } \]

This version avoids special-casing \(l=0\).

docs.title: 13. Prefix/Suffix Maximum
docs.text:
For:

nums = [3, 1, 5, 2, 4]

prefix maximum:

[3, 3, 5, 5, 5]

suffix maximum:

[5, 5, 5, 4, 4]

Useful for:

  • trapping rain water,
  • left/right maximum problems,
  • dominance relationships,
  • range maximum reasoning.

docs.title: 14. Pattern: Difference Array
docs.text:
For range updates:

\[ [l,r] \]

add \(x\).

Instead of modifying every element:

diff[l] += x

if r + 1 < n:
    diff[r + 1] -= x

Then reconstruct using a prefix sum.

This transforms:

\[ O(n) \]

per update into:

\[ O(1) \]

per update.

If there are \(q\) updates:

\[ O(q+n) \]

instead of potentially:

\[ O(qn). \]

docs.title: 16. Two Sum on a Sorted Array
25. Pattern: Sorting + Scanning
docs.text:
Sometimes the original order does not matter.

Sorting costs:

\[ O(n\log n) \]

but can expose structure that allows a simple linear scan.

Common problems:

  • 3Sum,
  • merging intervals,
  • grouping values,
  • duplicate detection,
  • closest pairs,
  • greedy scheduling.

General strategy:

unsorted array
      ↓
    sort
      ↓
exploit ordering
      ↓
   linear scan

docs.title: 26. 3Sum Pattern
docs.text:
Sort:

nums.sort()

Fix one element:

for i in range(n):

Then solve the remaining two-sum problem with two pointers.

Complexity:

\[ O(n\log n)+O(n^2) \]

therefore:

\[ \boxed{O(n^2)} \]

A crucial optimization is skipping duplicates:

if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
    continue

and similarly for the two pointers.

docs.title: 27. Pattern: Hashing
docs.text:
If we need fast membership:

seen = set()

Average complexity:

\[ O(1) \]

per lookup.

Typical pattern:

for x in nums:
    if x in seen:
        ...
    seen.add(x)

Useful for:

  • duplicates,
  • Two Sum,
  • longest consecutive sequence,
  • complement lookup,
  • frequency problems.

Trade-off:

\[ \text{Time} \downarrow \]

at the cost of:

\[ \text{Space} \uparrow \]

docs.title: 28. Pattern: Complement Lookup
docs.text:
For Two Sum:

\[ a+b=T \]

Rearrange:

\[ b=T-a \]

Therefore, while processing \(a\), search for:

\[ T-a. \] 
seen = {}

for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    complement = target - x

    if complement in seen:
        return [seen[complement], i]

    seen[x] = i

Average:

\[ O(n) \]

time.

Space:

\[ O(n) \]

docs.title: 29. Pattern: Kadane's Algorithm
docs.text:
Maximum subarray sum.

Define:

\[ bestEndingHere(i) \]

as the maximum sum of a subarray ending at \(i\).

Then:

\[ dp[i] = \max \left( A[i], dp[i-1]+A[i] \right) \]

The answer is:

\[ \max_i dp[i]. \]

We only need the previous state:

current = nums[0]
best = nums[0]

for x in nums[1:]:
    current = max(x, current + x)
    best = max(best, current)

Time:

\[ O(n) \]

Space:

\[ O(1) \]

docs.title: 30. Pattern: Monotonic Stack
docs.text:
Use when the problem asks for relationships with the:

  • next greater element,
  • next smaller element,
  • previous greater element,
  • previous smaller element.

Example:

A = [2,1,5,3]

For each element, we may want the first larger element to its right.

A monotonic stack maintains elements in sorted order.

Typical complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

Why?

Every element is:

  • pushed at most once,
  • popped at most once.

Therefore total stack operations are:

\[ O(n). \]

docs.title: 31. Pattern: Monotonic Deque
docs.text:
Useful when we need:

maximum/minimum over a moving window.

Example:

[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7]

with window size \(k\).

A deque can maintain candidates in decreasing order.

The front always contains the maximum candidate.

Each element enters and leaves the deque at most once.

Therefore:

\[ \boxed{O(n)} \]

docs.title: 32. Pattern: Intervals
docs.text:
An interval is:

\[ [l,r] \]

Typical problems:

  • merge intervals,
  • insert interval,
  • overlapping intervals,
  • meeting rooms,
  • interval scheduling.

Usually:

intervals.sort()

Then scan from left to right.

Sorting provides:

\[ l_1\le l_2\le\cdots \]

which makes overlap relationships easier to reason about.

docs.title: 33. Interval Overlap
docs.text:
Two intervals:

\[ [a,b] \]

and:

\[ [c,d] \]

overlap if:

\[ a\le d \]

and:

\[ c\le b. \]

Equivalently:

\[ \max(a,c)\le\min(b,d). \]

This identity is worth remembering.

docs.title: 34. Pattern: Cyclic Sort / Index Placement
docs.text:
Useful when:

  • numbers are in a restricted range,
  • values correspond to indices,
  • we need \(O(1)\) auxiliary space.

For example:

\[ 1\le A[i]\le n. \]

The desired position of value \(x\) is often:

\[ x-1. \]

So:

while nums[i] != i + 1:
    ...

This pattern appears in:

  • Missing Number,
  • Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array,
  • First Missing Positive,
  • Find the Duplicate Number.

docs.title: 35. Pattern: In-Place Marking
docs.text:
If values are restricted to indices, use the array itself as memory.

For example, if:

\[ 1\le x\le n \]

we can mark index \(x-1\).

A common trick:

nums[abs(x) - 1] *= -1

The sign stores additional information.

This can reduce:

\[ O(n)\text{ auxiliary space} \]

to:

\[ O(1). \]

Be careful when modifying the array because the original values may be needed later.

docs.title: 36. Pattern: Dutch National Flag
docs.text:
For arrays containing three categories, for example:

0, 1, 2

maintain three regions:

[0 ... low-1]
[low ... mid-1]
[mid ... high]
[high+1 ... n-1]

Maintain invariant:

0-region | 1-region | unknown | 2-region

The algorithm runs in:

\[ O(n) \]

time and:

\[ O(1) \]

space.

docs.title: 37. Pattern: Majority Element
docs.text:
If an element appears more than:

\[ \frac n2 \]

times, use Boyer-Moore Voting.

Maintain:

candidate
count

When:

\[ count=0 \]

choose a new candidate.

Otherwise:

same candidate → count + 1
different       → count - 1

The intuition is cancellation.

Pairs of different elements cancel each other.

A true majority cannot be completely cancelled.

Complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

time.

\[ O(1) \]

space.

docs.title: 38. Pattern: Prefix + Hash Map
docs.text:
A powerful combination.

Suppose:

\[ prefix[i]=\sum_{j=0}^{i}A[j]. \]

For a subarray sum equal to \(k\):

\[ prefix[r]-prefix[l]=k \]

which means:

\[ prefix[l]=prefix[r]-k. \]

Therefore, while scanning the array, store frequencies of previous prefix sums.

count = {0: 1}
prefix = 0
answer = 0

for x in nums:
    prefix += x

    answer += count.get(prefix - k, 0)

    count[prefix] = count.get(prefix, 0) + 1

Average complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

This technique is extremely important for subarray-sum problems, especially when negative numbers are present.

docs.title: 39. Pattern: Greedy Scanning
docs.text:
Sometimes a locally optimal decision can be proven to lead to a globally optimal result.

Examples include:

  • Jump Game,
  • Gas Station,
  • interval scheduling,
  • maximum subarray variants.

Do not use greedy merely because it "looks right".

Ask:

Why can the discarded alternatives never produce a better solution?

A greedy solution should have a correctness argument.

docs.title: 40. Pattern: Dynamic Programming on Arrays
docs.text:
Many DP problems define a state based on an index.

Typical form:

\[ dp[i] = f(dp[i-1],dp[i-2],\ldots,A[i]) \]

Examples:

  • House Robber,
  • Maximum Subarray,
  • Climbing Stairs,
  • Decode Ways.

The important questions are:

  1. What does \(dp[i]\) mean?
  2. What previous states can produce \(dp[i]\)?
  3. What is the recurrence?
  4. What are the base cases?
  5. Can the state be compressed?

docs.title: 41. Pattern: Divide and Conquer
docs.text:
Split:

\[ A \]

into smaller portions.

Typical structure:

          A
        /   \
       L     R
      / \   / \
     ...   ...

Solve each part and combine.

Examples:

  • Merge Sort,
  • inversion counting,
  • maximum subarray,
  • divide-and-conquer selection.

The classic recurrence:

\[ T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) \]

gives:

\[ \boxed{T(n)=O(n\log n)} \]

docs.title: 42. Pattern: Coordinate Compression
docs.text:
Suppose values are huge:

[10^9, 500, 10^7, 500]

but only their relative ordering matters.

Sort unique values:

[500, 10^7, 10^9]

Map:

500   → 0
10^7  → 1
10^9  → 2

Now large values become compact indices.

Useful for:

  • Fenwick trees,
  • segment trees,
  • frequency arrays,
  • interval problems,
  • sweep line algorithms.

docs.title: 43. Pattern: Sweep Line
docs.text:
Convert an interval problem into events.

For interval:

\[ [l,r] \]

create:

(l, +1)
(r, -1)

Sort events.

Then scan from left to right while maintaining the active count.

Useful for:

  • maximum overlapping intervals,
  • meeting rooms,
  • range coverage,
  • geometric problems.

docs.title: 44. Pattern: Matrix / 2D Array
docs.text:
A matrix is simply a multidimensional array.

For:

\[ A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} \]

each element is:

\[ A[i][j]. \]

Common patterns:

  • row traversal,
  • column traversal,
  • diagonal traversal,
  • spiral traversal,
  • matrix rotation,
  • transpose,
  • flood fill,
  • prefix sums,
  • binary search.

docs.title: 45. 2D Prefix Sum
docs.text:
Define:

\[ P[i][j] = \sum_{x\le i}\sum_{y\le j}A[x][y]. \]

Then a rectangle sum can be calculated using inclusion-exclusion.

For rectangle:

\[ (r_1,c_1)\rightarrow(r_2,c_2) \]

the sum is:

\[ P[r_2][c_2] -P[r_1-1][c_2] -P[r_2][c_1-1] +P[r_1-1][c_1-1]. \]

The final addition is necessary because the top-left region was subtracted twice.

docs.title: Reverse in-place
docs.text:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1

while l < r:
    nums[l], nums[r] = nums[r], nums[l]
    l += 1
    r -= 1

Time:

\[ O(n) \]

Space:

\[ O(1) \]

docs.title: Swap Without Extra Array
docs.text:
Python:

a, b = b, a

docs.title: Rotate Array
docs.text:
A rotation can be performed using reversals.

For right rotation by \(k\):

reverse entire array
reverse first k
reverse remaining n-k

Always normalize:

k %= n

because:

\[ k\equiv k\bmod n \]

for rotations.

docs.title: 47. Avoiding Off-by-One Errors
docs.text:
Always explicitly define whether your interval is:

\[ [l,r] \]

or:

\[ [l,r) \]

For Python slicing:

nums[l:r]

means:

\[ [l,r) \]

because \(r\) is excluded.

A large number of binary-search and sliding-window bugs are boundary-definition bugs rather than algorithmic bugs.

docs.title: 48. Useful Index Identities
docs.text: For an array of length \(n\):

docs.title: Number of elements in inclusive interval
Number of elements in half-open interval
Middle
docs.text:
\[ mid=l+\left\lfloor\frac{r-l}{2}\right\rfloor \]

This form avoids overflow in languages where integer overflow is possible.

docs.title: Nested loops do not automatically mean \(O(n^2)\)
docs.text:
Consider:

l = 0

for r in range(n):
    while l < r:
        l += 1

Although there is a for and a while, \(l\) increases at most \(n\) times.

Therefore:

\[ O(n+n)=O(n). \]

Always count total pointer movement, not merely nesting depth.

docs.title: 50. Another Important Trap
docs.text:
This:

for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i, n):
        ...

does have:

\[ n+(n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1 \]

iterations.

Therefore:

\[ \frac{n(n+1)}2 \]

and hence:

\[ \boxed{O(n^2)}. \]

docs.title: 51. In-Place vs Auxiliary Space
docs.text:
If an algorithm modifies the input array:

nums[i] = ...

that does not necessarily count as auxiliary space.

For example:

reverse(nums)

can use:

\[ O(1) \]

auxiliary space.

But creating:

result = []

of size \(n\) requires:

\[ O(n) \]

space.

Always distinguish:

  • input space,
  • output space,
  • auxiliary space.

docs.title: 52. When You See These Words...
docs.text:
Problem wording Consider "sorted" Binary search / two pointers "pair" Hashing / two pointers "subarray" Prefix sum / sliding window / Kadane "range sum" Prefix sum "range update" Difference array "next greater" Monotonic stack "window maximum" Monotonic deque "frequency" Hash map / frequency array "values from 1 to n" Index marking / cyclic sort "minimum possible" Binary search on answer "maximum possible" Binary search / greedy / DP "intervals" Sort + scan / sweep line "three values" Dutch National Flag "majority" Boyer-Moore "contiguous" Sliding window / prefix / DP "in-place" Two pointers / index marking "closest pair" Sorting + two pointers "all combinations" Backtracking "overlapping ranges" Sweep line "repeated range queries" Prefix/suffix preprocessing

These are hints, not rules.

docs.title: 53. The Most Important Question
docs.text:
When solving an array problem, do not immediately ask:

"Which LeetCode pattern is this?"

Instead ask:

docs.title: 1. What information does the problem require?
docs.text:
Is it asking about:

  • individual elements?
  • pairs?
  • subarrays?
  • prefixes?
  • frequencies?
  • ranges?
  • ordering?

docs.title: 2. What structure does the input provide?
docs.text:
Is it:

  • sorted?
  • bounded?
  • positive?
  • distinct?
  • duplicated?
  • circular?
  • partially ordered?

docs.title: 3. What information can be maintained?
docs.text:
Can I maintain:

\[ sum \] \[ min \] \[ max \] \[ frequency \] \[ prefix \] \[ window \] \[ candidate \] \[ stack \]

docs.title: 4. What can be eliminated?
docs.text:
A good algorithm usually wins by eliminating possibilities.

Binary search eliminates half.

Two pointers eliminate regions.

Hashing eliminates repeated searches.

Prefix sums eliminate repeated summation.

Monotonic stacks eliminate dominated candidates.

Dynamic programming eliminates repeated subproblems.

docs.title: 54. Array Problem-Solving Checklist
docs.text:
Before coding:

  • [ ] What exactly is the input?
  • [ ] Is it sorted?
  • [ ] Are values bounded?
  • [ ] Are duplicates allowed?
  • [ ] Can values be negative?
  • [ ] Is the answer about a contiguous range?
  • [ ] Do I need pairs?
  • [ ] Can I preprocess?
  • [ ] Can I use a hash map?
  • [ ] Can I use two pointers?
  • [ ] Is there a monotonic predicate?
  • [ ] Can I binary-search the answer?
  • [ ] Can I maintain a running state?
  • [ ] Can I solve it in-place?
  • [ ] What invariant does my loop maintain?
  • [ ] What is the time complexity?
  • [ ] What is the auxiliary-space complexity?
  • [ ] What happens at \(n=0\)?
  • [ ] What happens at \(n=1\)?
  • [ ] What happens with duplicates?
  • [ ] What happens with negative values?
  • [ ] What happens at the boundaries?

docs.title: 56. Final Mental Model
docs.text: Think of an array at four different levels.

docs.title: Level 1 — Mathematical
docs.text:
\[ A:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\rightarrow S \]

It is a finite sequence/function.

docs.title: Level 2 — Memory
docs.text:
\[ \operatorname{address}(A[i])=B+iw \]

It is contiguous memory plus address arithmetic.

docs.title: Level 3 — Algorithmic
docs.text:
Exploit properties such as:

\[ \text{ordering} \] \[ \text{contiguity} \] \[ \text{monotonicity} \] \[ \text{frequency} \] \[ \text{prefix structure} \] \[ \text{locality} \]

docs.title: Level 4 — Problem Solving
docs.text:
Transform the problem:

Raw Array
    ↓
Identify structure
    ↓
Choose representation
    ↓
Maintain an invariant/state
    ↓
Eliminate unnecessary work
    ↓
Prove correctness
    ↓
Analyze complexity

The goal is not to memorize that:

"This is a two-pointer problem."

The goal is to understand why two pointers are valid.

Likewise, do not memorize:

"Prefix sum = O(1)."

Understand that preprocessing changes:

\[ \text{repeated computation} \]

into:

\[ \text{one-time computation}+\text{constant-time queries}. \]

That way, when you encounter a problem you have never seen before, you can derive the technique instead of trying to recognize a memorized solution.

docs.title: Sliding Window
docs.text: These

docs.title: 17. Pattern: Sliding Window
docs.text:
A sliding window maintains an interval:

\[ [l,r] \] 
       l           r
       ↓           ↓
A = [ x ][ x ][ x ][ x ][ x ][ x ]
       └───────────┘
          window

Typical structure:

l = 0

for r in range(n):

    # add nums[r]

    while condition_is_invalid:
        # remove nums[l]
        l += 1

    # process window

If both \(l\) and \(r\) move only forward:

\[ l\le n \]

and

\[ r\le n. \]

Therefore total pointer movement is at most:

\[ 2n \]

giving:

\[ \boxed{O(n)} \]

docs.title: 18. Fixed-Size Sliding Window
docs.text:
If the window has fixed size \(k\):

\[ A[i-k+1:i+1] \]

Maintain its sum:

window_sum = sum(nums[:k])

for r in range(k, n):
    window_sum += nums[r]
    window_sum -= nums[r-k]

Each step performs constant work.

Therefore:

\[ O(n) \]

instead of:

\[ O(nk). \]

docs.title: 19. Variable-Size Sliding Window
docs.text:
Typical problem:

Find the longest/shortest subarray satisfying some condition.

Structure:

l = 0

for r in range(n):

    add(nums[r])

    while invalid():
        remove(nums[l])
        l += 1

    update_answer()

The crucial requirement is that the validity condition should allow the left pointer to move monotonically.

docs.title: 20. Sliding Window Warning
docs.text:
Do not automatically use sliding window just because the problem says "subarray".

Sliding window works when the condition has the right monotonic behavior.

For example, with positive numbers:

\[ sum([l,r]) \]

increases when \(r\) increases and decreases when \(l\) increases.

This property often makes sliding window possible.

With arbitrary negative numbers, that monotonicity can disappear.

docs.title: 15. Pattern: Two Pointers
docs.text:
Use two indices:

l = 0
r = len(nums) - 1

and move them according to some property.

Common form:

while l < r:
    ...

Two pointers are especially useful when:

  • the array is sorted,
  • the problem involves pairs,
  • the answer depends on both ends,
  • a pointer movement eliminates possibilities.

docs.title: 16. Two Sum on a Sorted Array
docs.text:
Suppose:

[1,2,4,6,8,9]

and target:

\[ 10 \]

Start:

l →              ← r

If:

\[ A[l]+A[r] > target \]

decrease \(r\).

If:

\[ A[l]+A[r] < target \]

increase \(l\).

Why is this valid?

Because the array is sorted.

If:

\[ A[l]+A[r]>T \]

then for the current \(r\):

\[ A[l+1]+A[r]\ge A[l]+A[r]>T \]

so \(r\) cannot pair with any index to the right of \(l\).

This is the kind of reasoning you should look for:

Can a pointer movement eliminate an entire set of candidates?

docs.title: Hashing: The 7 Core Patterns in DSA
docs.text:
Hashing is a technique that allows us to store information in a way that makes searching, counting, and retrieving data efficient.

In Python, the two primary data structures used for hashing are:

  • set: Stores unique elements and supports fast membership testing.
  • dict: Stores key-value pairs and supports fast lookup by key.

Both typically provide \(O(1)\) average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion, although worst-case performance can be \(O(n)\).

Let's understand the seven patterns one by one, starting with the fundamentals and progressing toward advanced applications.

docs.title: Sets, maps, membership, and frequency counting
docs.text:
Basic hashing is the foundation of almost every other hashing pattern.

The central idea is:

Instead of repeatedly searching through an entire collection, store information in a hash-based data structure so that you can retrieve it efficiently.

docs.title: 1.1 Membership Testing
docs.text:
Problem: Determine whether an element exists in a collection.

Suppose we have:

nums = [4, 7, 2, 9, 5]
target = 9

docs.title: Approach 1: Linear Search
docs.text:
found = False

for x in nums:
    if x == target:
        found = True
        break

In the worst case, we inspect every element.

Time complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

docs.title: Approach 2: Hash Set
docs.text:
seen = set(nums)

found = target in seen

Building the set takes \(O(n)\) expected time, and the membership check takes \(O(1)\) average time.

If the set already exists, the lookup itself is expected \(O(1)\).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use a hash set when you need to answer questions like:

  • Does this value exist?
  • Have I seen this element before?
  • Is this element a duplicate?
  • Is a particular state already visited?

docs.title: 1.2 Duplicate Detection
docs.text:
Problem: Determine whether an array contains duplicate elements.

Example:

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 2]

docs.title: Hashing solution
docs.text:
def contains_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()

    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True

        seen.add(x)

    return False

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Element Set before processing Result 1 {} Insert 1 2 {1} Insert 2 3 {1, 2} Insert 3 4 {1, 2, 3} Insert 4 2 {1, 2, 3, 4} Duplicate found

Expected time complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

Auxiliary space complexity:

\[ O(n) \]

Key insight: A set remembers which elements have already appeared.

docs.title: 1.3 Frequency Counting
docs.text:
Problem: Count how many times each element occurs.

Example:

nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]

Expected output:

{
    1: 1,
    2: 2,
    3: 3
}

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def frequency_count(nums):
    freq = {}

    for x in nums:
        freq[x] = freq.get(x, 0) + 1

    return freq

The expression:

freq.get(x, 0)

returns the current count of x, or 0 if the key does not exist.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(k)\), where \(k\) is the number of distinct elements.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Frequency counting is useful for:

  • Finding the most frequent element.
  • Checking whether two strings are anagrams.
  • Counting pairs with certain properties.
  • Identifying elements that occur exactly once.

docs.title: 1.4 Frequency Map Equality
docs.text:
Suppose we want to determine whether two strings are anagrams.

s = "listen"
t = "silent"

Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies.

from collections import Counter

def is_anagram(s, t):
    return Counter(s) == Counter(t)

This is a direct application of frequency counting.

docs.title: Summary of Basic Hashing
docs.text: Pattern Data structure Main purpose Membership testing Set Check existence Duplicate detection Set Detect repeated values Frequency counting Dictionary Count occurrences Frequency comparison Dictionary Compare distributions

docs.title: Complement lookup, index mapping, and pair counting
docs.text:
Array hashing uses a hash map or set to solve problems involving relationships between array elements.

The most important idea is:

Instead of searching the array repeatedly, store information about previously processed elements.

docs.title: 2.1 Complement Lookup
docs.text: This pattern is best illustrated by the classic Two Sum problem.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given an array and a target, find two elements whose sum equals the target.

nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]
target = 9

We need:

\[ a+b=target \]

Rearranging:

\[ b=target-a \]

This means that for every element \(a\), we can calculate the exact value of its required complement.

docs.title: Brute-force approach
docs.text:
for i in range(len(nums)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
        if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
            return [i, j]

Time complexity:

\[ O(n^2) \]

docs.title: Hashing approach
docs.text:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}

    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        complement = target - x

        if complement in seen:
            return [seen[complement], i]

        seen[x] = i

    return []

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
Current element Complement Map before lookup Result 2 7 {} Store 2 7 2 {2: 0} Found 2

The answer is:

[0, 1]

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(n)\).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Look for equations that can be rearranged into:

\[ \text{Required value} = \text{Target} - \text{Current value} \]

This pattern also applies to difference-based and product-based pair problems, although the exact lookup strategy may differ.

docs.title: 2.2 Index Mapping
docs.text:
Sometimes we need to know not only whether an element exists, but also where it occurs.

For example:

nums = [10, 20, 30, 20, 40]

We can map each value to its most recent index.

index_map = {}

for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    index_map[x] = i

Result:

{
    10: 0,
    20: 3,
    30: 2,
    40: 4
}

Notice that the index of 20 is 3, because the most recent occurrence overwrites the earlier one.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
First occurrence:

if x not in index_map:
    index_map[x] = i

Last occurrence:

index_map[x] = i

All occurrences:

index_map.setdefault(x, []).append(i)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Index mapping is useful for:

  • Finding the distance between repeated elements.
  • Locating previous occurrences.
  • Finding the first or last occurrence.
  • Solving problems involving pairs of indices.

docs.title: 2.3 Pair Counting
docs.text:
This pattern counts pairs satisfying a mathematical condition.

Suppose:

nums = [1, 5, 7, -1, 5]
target = 6

We want to count pairs whose sum equals 6.

The key equation is:

\[ a+b=target \]

For each current element \(b\), we look for:

\[ a=target-b \]

Instead of storing just whether a value exists, we store how many times it has appeared.

def count_pairs(nums, target):
    freq = {}
    count = 0

    for x in nums:
        complement = target - x

        count += freq.get(complement, 0)

        freq[x] = freq.get(x, 0) + 1

    return count

For this example, the answer is 3.

The pairs are:

  • (1, 5) using the first 5.
  • (1, 5) using the second 5.
  • (7, -1).

Each pair is counted once because the map contains only previously processed elements.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(k)\), where \(k\) is the number of distinct elements.

docs.title: Prefix sums, prefix XOR, and subarray counting
docs.text:
This is one of the most powerful hashing patterns in DSA.

It combines two ideas:

  1. Prefix computations.
  2. Hash maps that store previously encountered prefix states.

The result is an efficient way to solve many subarray problems.

docs.title: 3.1 Understanding Prefix Sums
docs.text:
Consider:

nums = [2, 4, 1, 3]

Define the prefix sum:

\[ P_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i}a_j \]

The prefix sums are:

Index Element Prefix sum 0 2 2 1 4 6 2 1 7 3 3 10

The prefix array is:

[2, 6, 7, 10]

The sum of a subarray from index \(l\) to \(r\) is:

\[ S(l,r)=P_r-P_{l-1} \]

If we define \(P_{-1}=0\), the formula works uniformly:

\[ S(l,r)=P_r-P_{l-1} \]

docs.title: Problem: Subarray Sum Equals K
docs.text:
Given an array, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals \(k\).

Example:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
k = 3

The valid subarrays are:

  • [1, 2]
  • [3]

Answer:

2

docs.title: Mathematical derivation
docs.text:
We want:

\[ P_r-P_l=k \]

Rearrange:

\[ P_l=P_r-k \]

At every position, we need to know how many earlier prefix sums equal:

\[ P_r-k \]

This is exactly what a hash map can provide.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    freq = {0: 1}
    prefix = 0
    count = 0

    for x in nums:
        prefix += x

        count += freq.get(prefix - k, 0)

        freq[prefix] = freq.get(prefix, 0) + 1

    return count

docs.title: Why initialize freq = {0: 1}?
docs.text:
This represents the empty prefix before the array begins.

It allows us to count subarrays that start at index 0.

For example, if the first element itself equals k, then:

\[ P_r-k=0 \]

The initial frequency of zero ensures that this subarray is counted.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(n)\).

docs.title: 3.3 Longest Subarray with Sum K
docs.text:
The same mathematical relationship can solve a different problem.

Instead of counting subarrays, we want the maximum length of a subarray whose sum equals \(k\).

For each prefix sum \(P_r\), we need an earlier prefix:

\[ P_l=P_r-k \]

The subarray length is:

\[ r-l \]

To maximize this length, we store the earliest index at which each prefix sum occurs.

def longest_subarray_sum_k(nums, k):
    first = {0: -1}
    prefix = 0
    best = 0

    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix += x

        target = prefix - k

        if target in first:
            best = max(best, i - first[target])

        if prefix not in first:
            first[prefix] = i

    return best

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Goal What to store Count valid subarrays Frequency of each prefix Find longest valid subarray Earliest index of each prefix Find shortest valid subarray Often latest suitable index, depending on constraints

The underlying mathematical relationship remains the same.

docs.title: 3.4 Prefix XOR + Hash Map
docs.text:
Prefix hashing also works with XOR.

Define:

\[ X_i=a_0\oplus a_1\oplus\cdots\oplus a_i \]

The XOR of a subarray is:

\[ X_r\oplus X_l \]

For a target XOR \(k\):

\[ X_r\oplus X_l=k \]

Rearranging:

\[ X_l=X_r\oplus k \]

Therefore, we can count subarrays with XOR \(k\) using a frequency map.

def count_subarrays_xor(nums, k):
    freq = {0: 1}
    prefix = 0
    count = 0

    for x in nums:
        prefix ^= x

        count += freq.get(prefix ^ k, 0)

        freq[prefix] = freq.get(prefix, 0) + 1

    return count

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Prefix hashing is especially useful when a problem asks for:

  • The number of subarrays with a given sum.
  • The longest subarray satisfying a sum condition.
  • Subarrays with zero sum.
  • Subarrays with a given XOR.
  • Subarrays whose sum is divisible by a number.

docs.title: Sliding windows with sets and frequency maps
docs.text:
Window hashing combines a sliding window with a hash-based data structure.

The sliding window determines which elements are currently relevant.

The hash map or set maintains information about those elements.

docs.title: Problem: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
docs.text:
Given a string, find the length of the longest substring containing no repeated characters.

Example:

s = "abcabcbb"

Answer:

3

The longest valid substrings include "abc", "bca", and "cab".

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Maintain a window:

\[ [l,r] \]

such that every character inside the window is unique.

When a duplicate appears, move the left boundary until the window becomes valid again.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = set()
    left = 0
    best = 0

    for right, char in enumerate(s):

        while char in seen:
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1

        seen.add(char)

        best = max(best, right - left + 1)

    return best

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(k)\), where \(k\) is the number of distinct characters in the active window.

Each character enters and leaves the window at most once.

docs.title: Problem: Find All Anagrams in a String
docs.text:
Given two strings, find all starting indices where an anagram of the second string appears in the first.

s = "cbaebabacd"
p = "abc"

Answer:

[0, 6]

The substrings "cba" and "bac" are anagrams of "abc".

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
An anagram is determined by character frequencies.

We maintain:

  • A frequency map for the target string.
  • A frequency map for the current window.

If the two frequency distributions match, the window is an anagram.

docs.title: Python solution
docs.text:
from collections import Counter

def find_anagrams(s, p):
    if len(p) > len(s):
        return []

    target = Counter(p)
    window = Counter(s[:len(p)])

    ans = []

    if window == target:
        ans.append(0)

    for right in range(len(p), len(s)):
        entering = s[right]
        leaving = s[right - len(p)]

        window[entering] += 1
        window[leaving] -= 1

        if window[leaving] == 0:
            del window[leaving]

        if window == target:
            ans.append(right - len(p) + 1)

    return ans

This is a straightforward implementation. Comparing entire frequency maps at every step may cost more than constant time when the alphabet is large.

For a fixed, small alphabet, we can optimize by tracking how many character frequencies currently match.

docs.title: When to use window hashing
docs.text:
Use this combination when:

  • You need to track unique elements in a window.
  • You need character frequencies in a substring.
  • You need to find anagrams.
  • You need to count distinct elements in a moving range.
  • You need to maintain a frequency-based condition as the window changes.

docs.title: Anagram signatures, rolling hash, and Rabin–Karp
docs.text:
String hashing has two major branches:

  1. Structural hashing: Represent a string using a property such as its character frequencies.
  2. Rolling hashing: Represent a string or substring using a numerical hash value.

These solve different types of problems.

docs.title: Problem: Group Anagrams
docs.text:
Given:

strs = ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]

We need to group strings that are anagrams of one another.

docs.title: Key observation
docs.text:
Anagrams contain the same characters with the same frequencies.

Therefore, we can create a canonical representation of each string.

For lowercase English letters, the signature can be a tuple of 26 character frequencies.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(strs):
    groups = defaultdict(list)

    for word in strs:
        freq = [0] * 26

        for char in word:
            freq[ord(char) - ord('a')] += 1

        key = tuple(freq)

        groups[key].append(word)

    return list(groups.values())

docs.title: Why use a tuple?
docs.text:
A tuple is immutable and hashable, so it can be used as a dictionary key.

The frequency array itself is mutable and cannot be used directly as a dictionary key.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
For \(n\) strings with an average length of \(m\):

  • Time: \(O(nm)\) for a fixed alphabet.
  • Space: Depends on the number of distinct signatures and stored strings.

docs.title: 5.2 Rolling Hash
docs.text:
Rolling hash is used to compute hash values for substrings efficiently.

Suppose we have:

s = "abcdef"

We want to compare many substrings without repeatedly processing every character.

A polynomial rolling hash can be defined as:

\[ H(s)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}s_i p^i \pmod m \]

Where:

  • \(s_i\) is a numerical representation of a character.
  • \(p\) is a base.
  • \(m\) is a modulus.

With suitable prefix-hash and power arrays, we can compute a substring hash in \(O(1)\) time after \(O(n)\) preprocessing.

docs.title: Why is this useful?
docs.text:
Suppose we want to compare two substrings of length \(L\).

Without hashing, comparing them directly may take:

\[ O(L) \]

With prefix hashes, comparing their hash values takes:

\[ O(1) \]

However, hash collisions are possible, so equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings.

docs.title: 5.3 Rabin–Karp
docs.text: Rabin–Karp is a string-searching algorithm that uses rolling hashes.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Find occurrences of a pattern inside a text.

For example:

text = "ababcabc"
pattern = "abc"

We want to find the positions where "abc" occurs.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
1. Compute the hash of the pattern.
  2. Compute the hash of the first text window of the same length.
  3. Compare the hashes.
  4. Slide the window and update its hash efficiently.
  5. If hashes match, verify the actual characters to guard against collisions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
With a well-behaved hash and appropriate implementation:

  • Expected time: \(O(n+m)\) for a single pattern of length \(m\) in text of length \(n\).
  • Worst-case time can be higher due to collisions and verification.

docs.title: When to use string hashing
docs.text:
Use it for:

  • Finding repeated substrings.
  • Detecting duplicate strings.
  • Comparing substrings efficiently.
  • Pattern matching.
  • Longest duplicate substring problems.

docs.title: Remainders, bitmasks, and state representations
docs.text:
Mathematical hashing uses mathematical transformations to create compact keys that represent values, relationships, or states.

The key idea is:

Transform a complicated property into a simpler representation that can be stored and retrieved using a hash map.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Count pairs whose sum is divisible by \(k\).

For two integers \(a\) and \(b\):

\[ (a+b)\bmod k=0 \]

This is equivalent to:

\[ (a\bmod k+b\bmod k)\bmod k=0 \]

Let:

\[ r=a\bmod k \]

Then the complementary remainder is:

\[ (k-r)\bmod k \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
k = 5

The remainders are:

[1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1]

A remainder of 1 pairs with a remainder of 4.

A remainder of 2 pairs with a remainder of 3.

A remainder of 0 pairs with another remainder of 0.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def count_pairs_divisible_by_k(nums, k):
    freq = {}
    count = 0

    for x in nums:
        r = x % k
        complement = (-r) % k

        count += freq.get(complement, 0)

        freq[r] = freq.get(r, 0) + 1

    return count

This counts unordered pairs of distinct indices.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(k)\) in the worst case, because there are at most \(k\) possible remainders.

docs.title: 6.2 Bitmask Hashing
docs.text:
A bitmask represents a collection of Boolean properties using bits.

For example, if we want to represent which of the first four letters appear in a string:

Character Bit a 0001 b 0010 c 0100 d 1000

The string "ac" can be represented as:

\[ 0001 \;|\; 0100=0101 \]

This compact representation is useful for tracking character sets.

docs.title: Example: Unique Characters
docs.text:
def has_unique_chars(s):
    mask = 0

    for char in s:
        bit = 1 << (ord(char) - ord('a'))

        if mask & bit:
            return False

        mask |= bit

    return True

This works for lowercase English letters.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
For a string of length \(n\):

  • Time: \(O(n)\).
  • Auxiliary space: \(O(1)\) when the alphabet size is fixed and the bitmask fits in a constant number of machine words.

docs.title: 6.3 Bitmask + Hash Map
docs.text:
Bitmasks can also represent the parity of character frequencies.

Consider a string where we want to count substrings that contain at most one character with an odd frequency.

For each character:

  • Toggle its corresponding bit.
  • Store the frequency of each previously encountered mask.

If the current mask is \(M\), a substring has all-even character frequencies when the earlier mask is also \(M\).

For at most one odd-frequency character, the earlier mask can be:

\[ M \]

or:

\[ M\oplus 2^i \]

for one bit position \(i\).

This is the central idea behind problems such as Number of Wonderful Substrings.

docs.title: 6.4 State Representation
docs.text:
Sometimes a problem involves a complex state that needs to be tracked.

For example, in a lock puzzle, a state might be:

"1234"

A set can store visited states:

visited = {"1234", "1235", "1236"}

Before exploring a new state, check whether it has already been visited.

This is common in:

  • BFS.
  • DFS.
  • State-space search.
  • Puzzles.
  • Graph traversal.
  • Simulations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Pattern Transformation Typical use Remainder hashing Number → remainder Divisibility and pair counting Bitmask hashing Set of properties → integer Character sets and parity State hashing Complex state → hashable representation BFS, DFS, and simulations

docs.title: Dynamic programming, graphs, geometry, and data structure design
docs.text:
Advanced hashing combines hash maps and sets with other algorithms or data structures.

These patterns become especially useful when the problem requires storing more complex relationships.

docs.title: 7.1 Hashing + Dynamic Programming
docs.text:
Dynamic programming often involves repeatedly solving the same subproblem.

A hash map can store previously computed results.

docs.title: Example: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence
docs.text:
Given:

nums = [3, 6, 9, 12]

We want the longest subsequence in which the difference between consecutive elements is constant.

The answer is:

4

The difference is:

\[ d=3 \]

docs.title: DP state
docs.text:
Let:

\[ dp[i][d] \]

represent the length of the longest arithmetic subsequence ending at index \(i\) with common difference \(d\).

For each pair of indices \(j<i\):

\[ d=nums[i]-nums[j] \]

We extend the sequence ending at \(j\) with difference \(d\).

docs.title: Python solution
docs.text:
def longest_arith_seq_length(nums):
    n = len(nums)

    dp = [{} for _ in range(n)]
    best = 1

    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i):
            d = nums[i] - nums[j]

            length = dp[j].get(d, 1) + 1

            dp[i][d] = max(dp[i].get(d, 0), length)

            best = max(best, dp[i][d])

    return best

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(n^2)\) expected.
  • Space: \(O(n^2)\) in the worst case.

Key insight: A hash map allows each DP state to be indexed by a difference value without allocating a large array for every possible difference.

docs.title: 7.2 Hashing + Graphs
docs.text: Hash maps and sets are widely used to represent graphs and track visited nodes.

docs.title: Example: Clone Graph
docs.text:
Suppose we have a graph where each node has a value and a list of neighbors.

We need to create a deep copy of the graph.

The challenge is that multiple edges may point to the same node, and cycles may exist.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Use a map:

\[ original\ node \rightarrow cloned\ node \]

When visiting a node:

  1. Check whether its clone already exists.
  2. If it does, return the existing clone.
  3. Otherwise, create the clone.
  4. Recursively clone its neighbors.

docs.title: Python implementation
docs.text:
def clone_graph(node):
    if node is None:
        return None

    clones = {}

    def dfs(curr):
        if curr in clones:
            return clones[curr]

        copy = Node(curr.val)
        clones[curr] = copy

        for neighbor in curr.neighbors:
            copy.neighbors.append(dfs(neighbor))

        return copy

    return dfs(node)

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• Time: \(O(V+E)\).
  • Space: \(O(V)\) for the clone map, excluding the output graph and recursion stack.

Key insight: The hash map prevents duplicate cloning and handles cycles.

docs.title: 7.3 Hashing + Geometry
docs.text: Hashing is useful when geometric relationships can be represented as keys.

docs.title: Example: Detect Squares
docs.text:
Suppose we have a collection of points on a 2D plane.

We want to count how many axis-aligned squares can be formed using a given point as one of the corners.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Store point frequencies:

\[ (x,y)\rightarrow \text{frequency} \]

For a given point:

\[ (x_1,y_1) \]

and another point:

\[ (x_2,y_2) \]

that lies on the same horizontal line, we can determine the possible vertical coordinates of the other two corners.

The square's side length is:

\[ d=|x_2-x_1| \]

The remaining corners must lie at:

\[ (x_1,y_1+d),\quad (x_2,y_2+d) \]

or:

\[ (x_1,y_1-d),\quad (x_2,y_2-d) \]

A hash map lets us check whether these points exist and retrieve their frequencies.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use geometric hashing when:

  • Points have integer coordinates.
  • You need fast coordinate membership checks.
  • You need to count geometric configurations.
  • You need to group points by slopes or differences.

docs.title: 7.4 Hash Map + Doubly Linked List
docs.text: This combination is used in data structure design problems.

docs.title: Example: LRU Cache
docs.text:
An LRU cache removes the least recently used item when its capacity is exceeded.

We need:

  • Fast lookup by key.
  • Fast removal of the least recently used item.
  • Fast movement of an accessed item to the most-recently-used position.

A hash map alone cannot efficiently maintain recency order.

A doubly linked list alone cannot efficiently locate arbitrary keys.

Combining them solves both problems.

docs.title: Data structure
docs.text:
Hash Map:
key → linked-list node

Doubly Linked List:
Least Recently Used ↔ Most Recently Used

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Operation Expected time Get O(1) Put O(1) Remove least recently used O(1)

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
The hash map gives direct access to a node.

The doubly linked list allows that node to be removed and moved to the front in constant time.

This is a classic example of combining data structures to satisfy multiple complexity requirements.

docs.title: Final Summary: The 7 Hashing Patterns
docs.text: # Pattern Main idea Key application 1 Basic Hashing Store elements and their frequencies Membership and duplicate detection 2 Array Hashing Store values, indices, and complements Two Sum and pair counting 3 Prefix Hashing Store prefix states Subarray sum and XOR problems 4 Window Hashing Maintain information about a moving window Anagrams and unique substrings 5 String Hashing Represent and compare strings efficiently Group Anagrams and Rabin–Karp 6 Mathematical Hashing Transform values into compact mathematical states Remainders, bitmasks, and state search 7 Advanced Hashing Combine hashing with other algorithms and data structures DP, graphs, geometry, and LRU Cache

docs.title: How to Recognize Which Pattern to Use
docs.text:
When solving a new problem, ask these questions in order:

  1. Do I need to check whether an element exists? → Basic hashing.
  2. Do I need to find a pair or track indices? → Array hashing.
  3. Am I dealing with contiguous subarrays and cumulative values? → Prefix hashing.
  4. Am I maintaining a contiguous range that expands and shrinks? → Window hashing.
  5. Am I comparing strings, substrings, or character distributions? → String hashing.
  6. Can I transform the problem into remainders, bitmasks, or compact states? → Mathematical hashing.
  7. Do I need to combine hashing with DP, graphs, geometry, or another data structure? → Advanced hashing.

The most important progression is: Basic Hashing → Array Hashing → Prefix Hashing → Window Hashing → String Hashing → Mathematical Hashing → Advanced Hashing.
